title: ‘a et-tilifōn — calls, messages, and invitations
goal: Make and answer phone calls with the right formulas, write short messages, and invite and decline invitations without causing offense.
bekal: open and close a phone call with the usual formulas
write short messages with the abbreviations people in the Levant use

dialogs.title: حَكِي — عَزِيمِة عَ الْعَشَا
dialogs.intro: Laila calls Budi to invite him to dinner at her family's home on Friday.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: Fine, thanks. Am I disturbing you?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: إِمِّي بْتِعْزْمَك عَ الْعَشَا يَوْم الْجُمْعَة.
lines.id: My mom's inviting you to dinner on Friday.
lines.literal: mother-my she-invites-you to dinner day Friday.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: Really? Thanks so much. What time?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: حَوَالِي السَّبْعَة. بَسّ لَا تِتْأَخَّر، إِمِّي بْتِطْبُخ مَنْسَف.
lines.baca: hawaali es-sab‘a. bass la tit’akhkhar, immi btiṭbukh mansaf.
lines.id: Around seven. But don't be late, Mom's making mansaf.
lines.literal: around seven. but don't you-be-late, mother-my she-cooks mansaf.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.text: مَنْسَف؟ أَكِيد رَح إِجِي! بْجِيب شِي مَعِي؟
lines.baca: mansaf? akiid rah iji! bjiib shi ma‘i?
lines.id: Mansaf? I'm definitely coming! Should I bring anything?
lines.literal: mansaf? sure will I-come! I-bring something with-me?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: لَا وَاللَّه، مَا فِي دَاعِي. تَعَا إِنْتَ بَسّ.
lines.baca: la’ walla, ma fi daa‘i. ta‘a inta bass.
lines.literal: no by-God, not there-is reason. come you only.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: طَيِّب، جِيب حِلْوِيَّات إِذَا بَدَّك. بَسّ مِش لَازِم.
lines.baca: ṭayyib, jiib hilwiyyaat idha baddak. bass mish laazim.
lines.id: OK, bring some sweets if you like. But you don't have to.
lines.literal: good, bring sweets if want-you. but not must.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: OK. Will you send me the address on WhatsApp?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: Sure, I'll send it now. See you Friday.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: OK, say hi to your mom. Bye.

notes: **The formula for answering the phone hardly ever changes.** The person answering says أَلُو, and the caller gives their name with مَعَك… ("it's… speaking"). To a woman: مَعِك. Saying your own name first is basic politeness, even to someone who already has your number saved.

**The question عَم بِزْعِجَك؟ ("am I disturbing you?") is almost obligatory** at the start of a call, and the answer is always أَبَدًا ("not at all") — even when the person is busy. If you really can't talk, say فِيني إِحْكِيك بَعِد شْوَي؟

**⚠️ Telling a guest not to bring anything is part of the politeness dance, not a real "no."** When the host says مَا فِي دَاعِي, the right response isn't to obey but to bring something anyway. The phrase مَا بِصِير أَجِي إِيدِي فَاضْيِة ("I can't come empty-handed") is the key sentence, and saying it shows right away that you understand the customs.

**The word عَزَم means to invite, and عَزِيمِة means an invitation or a treat.** أَنَا عَازْمَك means "you're my guest" — and in a restaurant, it also means "I'm paying." The two meanings really are closely linked.

**The word بِصِير does double duty and is used all the time.** It means "happen," "become," and also "be OK, be proper." مَا بِصِير means "it's not right" or "you can't," and it's one of the gentlest ways to say no to something.

**Written messages in the Levant use the spoken language, not Standard Arabic.** People type كِيفَك، شُو أَخْبَارَك، هَلَّق on WhatsApp exactly as they say it. That's good news for you: what you learn in this book you can write straight away.

grammars.title: Phone formulas from start to finish
after: If the person isn't there, the answer is مِش مَوْجُود *mish mōjuud* ("not here"). To leave a message: مُمْكِن تْخَبْرُو إِنِّي اِتَّصَلِت؟ ("could you tell him I called?").
To ask for a call back: خَلِّيه يِتَّصِل فِيِّي ("have him call me"). The word خَلِّي from unit 14 appears again here, and the pattern خَلِّي + person + bare verb means "have him/her…".

grammars.title: Inviting, accepting, declining
after: The phrase شَرِّفْنَا literally means "honor us," and it's the warmest and most polite invitation there is. The reply: اَلشَّرَف إِلِي ("the honor is mine").

⚠️ Turning down a meal invitation needs a reason; "I can't" isn't enough. Give your reason (عِنْدِي اِمْتِحَان، عِنْدِي اِرْتِبَاط) and suggest another time. Declining without a reason sounds like you're rejecting the person, not the event.

Say it
Meaning
rows: how are you? how's it going?

blocks.text: The question وَين صِرِت؟ literally means "where have you got to," and it's the most natural way to ask where someone on the way is. Usual answers: قَرِيب ("close"), وَاصِل ("almost there"), or عَ الطَّرِيق ("on the way").

blocks.title: Abbreviations you'll see on screen
items: Arabic numerals **٢٣٧** and Western numerals are used side by side; don't be thrown when you see both in one message.
Young people often write Arabic in Latin letters — called *Arabizi*: **3** for ع, **7** for ح, **2** for hamza. So كيفك is written *kifak* and قهوة is written *2ahwe*.
The word **تِكْرَم** *tikram* is a polite reply to any request, like "you got it." Its long form is تِكْرَم عَيْنَك, which you met in unit 3.

sections.title: Small talk that closes a conversation

head: Levantine
Say it
Meaning
Reply
rows: your presence lights up the place

blocks.text: The phrase اِشْتَقْنَالَك ("we miss you") is said to anyone you haven't seen for a while, including acquaintances who aren't close. It's not a heavy declaration of feelings but warm politeness — and the reply is وْأَنَا أَكْتَر ("I miss you more").

blocks.title: Phone calls rarely get straight to the point
items: The order is almost always: greetings, how are you, how's the family, and only then the point. Skipping it feels rushed, or like something's wrong.
Hanging up happens in stages too: يَلَّا، سَلِّم عَ الْعِيلِة، اَللَّه يْخَلِّيك، بْشُوفَك — usually three or four sentences before it really ends.
If you're in a hurry, say so at the start: آسِف، أَنَا مِسْتَعْجِل شْوَي. People in the Levant will understand and get straight to the point.
My mom's inviting you to dinner.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
